author.name: Martha C. Nussbaum

essay_title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action
publication: Essay 5 in Aristotle's De Motu Animalium: Text with Translation, Commentary, and Interpretive Essays (Princeton University Press, 2nd ed. 1985), pp. 221-269

special_features: Originally drafted as part of Nussbaum's 1975 Harvard PhD thesis under G. E. L. Owen
Composed concurrently with Malcolm Schofield's 'Aristotle on the Imagination' (1978/1985); footnote 71 acknowledges parallel development
Epigraph from Henry James's The Portrait of a Lady (Isabel Archer)
Heavy footnote apparatus: 71 footnotes engaging modern Anglophone Aristotle scholarship + analytic philosophy of mind
Embedded Greek text in Greek alphabet at p.49 n.54 (rest of Greek is transliterated)
Engages contemporary philosophy of mind (Wittgenstein, Sartre, Ryle, Dennett, Goodman, Ishiguro, Nagel) as much as Aristotle commentary tradition (Ross, Hicks, Hamlyn, Rees, Freudenthal, Rodier)

section_structure.heading: Introduction (untitled)
section_structure.summary: Diagnoses the one-sidedness of prior phantasia scholarship, which has privileged DA III.3 + Parva Naturalia 'decaying-sense' passages over the action contexts of DA III.9-11 and De Motu Animalium. Argues that phantasia must be explained primarily as a faculty operative in action explanation. Mounts a four-part attack on the dominant 'image-theory' reading of Aristotelian phantasia, drawing on Wittgenstein, Sartre, Ishiguro, Dennett, and Goodman. Proposes that phantasia is best understood via its lexical kinship with phainesthai, as the faculty in virtue of which 'phainetai F' (something appears-F) registers for a sentient creature. Programmatic statement: phantasia is closer to 'seeing-as' than to internal picture-inspection.

section_structure.heading: Phantasia in the accounts of action
section_structure.summary: Surveys DA III.9-11 and MA 6-8 to demonstrate phantasia's central role in motivational explanation. Examines (a) MA 700b17 ff. listing phantasia among the kritika (distinction-making faculties) alongside aisthesis and nous; (b) MA 701a29-32 'drink' syllogism where any one of the three kritika can present the object; (c) MA 702a18 ff. where phantasia 'prepares' desire (the canonical statement of phantasia's umbrella role); (d) DA 432b15-16 motion requires both phantasia and desire; (e) DA 433b26-30 no desire without phantasia; (f) DA 433a31 phantasia same as aisthesis but different in einai. Concludes with the puzzle of phantasia/aisthesis identity: two aspects of one faculty, akin to arete/dikaiosune or road-up/road-down. Catalogs evidence (DA III.7-8, MA 701a, MA 703b18, MA 701b17-21, DA 431a14-17, DA 431b2 ff., DA 432a3-10) that thinking too is 'never without phantasma'.

section_structure.heading: The use and range of phantasia
section_structure.summary: Lexical-philological survey of phantasia/phantasma/phantazesthai in pre-Aristotelian (Aeschylus, Herodotus, Euripides, Plato — Theaetetus 152b-c, Sophist 235d-236b, Republic 596e-599a, Parmenides 166a, Symposium 211a, Philebus 38c) and Aristotelian usage. Establishes that phantasma in early Greek is the verbal noun of phainetai meaning 'what appears,' not 'image.' Traces Aristotle's broad usage in EN 1114a32 (phainomenon agathon), EE 1235b25-29, Insomn. 460b19 (sun appears a foot wide), Metaph. V.29 1024b17-26, Rhet. 1370b32 + 1371b19 (impression of superiority/being loved). Reads the controversial DA 428a1-4 'kata metaphoran' clause not as ruling out the phainetai-connected use but as bracketing the 'mere show / ostentatiousness' transferred sense (cf. Hdt. VII.10.5, Polybius, Rhet. 1404a11). Concedes the decaying-sense theory of memory (Mem. 450a25 ff., 451a15) and dreaming (Insomn. 461b29 ff.) involves image-language but shows MA 702a5 revises this with eidola-as-shadows. Concludes: even DA III.3's closing decaying-sense paragraph cannot govern III.3 as a whole; phantasia must be allowed broad scope.

section_structure.heading: Phantasia and aisthesis
section_structure.summary: Develops the positive thesis: phantasia is the interpretive aspect of perception. Confronts the passivity of Aristotelian aisthesis in DA II.12 (424a18-19, 424a21 ff. — aisthesis receives form without matter, like wax taking a signet-ring impress) where the proper object is quality (rose qua white) not substance (rose qua rose). To be moved to action the animal must perceive the man qua man, not qua pale; this object-as-F awareness is what phantasia adds. Confirmation passages: MA 701b17-21 (phantasia accompanied by bodily change), 701b19 ff., 703b19 ff. (forms of pleasant/painful), DA 432a9-10 (phantasmata like aisthemata 'without matter' = without passive impress), DA 429b20 ff. (judging things separately from matter = judging form). Crowning piece of evidence: DA II.8 420b31 ff. on voice — phone is semantikos only because it issues from a creature with phantasia, i.e., a creature whose utterance is about something. Yields the thesis-formula: 'reception and interpretation are not separable but thoroughly interdependent. There is no receptive innocent eye in perception.'

section_structure.heading: Phantasia and orexis
section_structure.summary: Phantasia is the animal's awareness of an object as desirable (or to-be-avoided). May present an object of desire in two moments: as the initial absent goal (thirst yields a phantasia of drink) and as the situational specification (a water fountain identified as drink). Practical delusion: dog seeing ammonia-solution as drink (parallel to non-practical 'sun seen as a foot wide'). Argues against treating phantasia as a behavioral disposition: it is a psychological process with theoretical physiological description, hence usable in explanation. Analyzes the two species of phantasia in DA III.11 (433b28): perceptual phantasia (shared with other animals) vs. deliberative/calculative phantasia (bouleutike, peculiar to rational creatures). Reads 434a7-10 ('one makes one phantasma out of many') not as Ross's 'collage of pictures' but as the rational creature's capacity to (1) see consequences as following from action and (2) measure consequence-sets against a single criterion. Phantasia ek syllogismou (DA 434a11) explains why only humans deliberate.

section_structure.heading: Phantasia and thinking
section_structure.summary: Addresses Aristotle's strongest claim: DA III.8 432a3-10 that all thinking — practical and theoretical — is accompanied by phantasmata. Reads this as the claim that thought always has some concrete vehicle of symbolization or envisaging (an example, a logical formalization, even words). The Mem. 449b31 ff. triangle case shows the symbolizing typically conveys 'unnecessary information' (a triangle of definite size). Nussbaum endorses the claim as empirical: 'God would not require phantasia.' Concedes Aristotle's exposition is uneven — the triangle example slips into picturing-as-similarity language. Closing paradigm-statement: 'the basic insight underlying the theory is the important one that perceptual reception is inseparable from interpretation.' As phainomena are the ground in scientific method, so the way the world looks to the creature (not unprocessed sensory material) is the explanatory ground in action theory. Final formula: 'perception, thought, and action all presuppose the exercise of phantasia.' Footnote 71 acknowledges Schofield's parallel paper.

outline: Cluster 1 (PDF 11-12, book 220-222): Nussbaum opens with the diagnosis that 'studies of Aristotle's theory of phantasia have often been one-sided.' Critics from Freudenthal onward have privileged the few decaying-sense passages of DA III.3 + the Parva Naturalia, treating the broader role of phantasia in DA III.9-11 and the De Motu Animalium as parasitic. Nussbaum reverses this priority: action passages are 'just as valuable evidence.' She introduces phainesthai as the etymological anchor for the entire phantasia-family.

Cluster 2 (PDF 13-14, book 223-224): The dominant 'image view' is stated as two claims: (1) phantasia always involves images that represent in virtue of similarity; (2) imagining involves the having of an image plus its inspection. Nussbaum traces the prevalence of this view to empiricist habits and to the ascription of image-theory to Aristotle by Ross, Hicks, Hamlyn, and Rees.

Cluster 3 (PDF 15-20, book 225-230): Four-part attack on the image view, marshaling Goodman's Languages of Art on representation-by-reference (not by similarity), Wittgenstein's Lectures on Religious Belief on convention, Sartre and Ishiguro on the active intentional character of imagining, and Dennett on the dream-tiger with countable stripes. Picasso's reply ('No matter; it will') anchors the thesis that representation is interpretation, not reproduction.

Cluster 4 (PDF 21, book 231): Transitional turn to Wittgenstein's 'seeing-as' as the proper analogue for Aristotle's phainetai. The 'phainomenon agathon' (EN III.4-5) is one's view of the good; phainomena are 'things in the world as seen and reported by human observers.' Programmatic claim: phantasia for Aristotle has scope as wide as phainomena, not the narrow scope of image-having.

Cluster 5 (PDF 22-24, book 232-234): Section I opens with MA 6's catalog of kritika (phantasia, aisthesis, nous/dianoia) at 700b17 ff., the 'drink' syllogism at 701a29-32 (any kritikon + desire = motion), and the umbrella passage at 702a18 ff. (phantasia prepares desire). DA 432b15 and 433b26-30 confirm: motion is always with both phantasia and desire; no desire without phantasia. DA III.11 admits 'incomplete creatures' have some indistinct phantasia because they move. The two species (perceptual + deliberative/bouleutike) are introduced.

Cluster 6 (PDF 25-26, book 234-236): The DA 433a31 + De Insomn. 459a15 claim that phantasia and aisthesis are 'the same but different in einai' is parsed through analogous einai-passages (Metaph. XI.10 1066a33 road up/down; Mem. 450b21 painted-animal qua likeness vs. qua animal; EN V 1130a12 arete/dikaiosune; EN VI 1143b23 phronesis/politike). Nussbaum extracts the 'two-description' reading: same capacity, two aspects under different descriptions. Not (a la road up/down) two activities of one power, but (a la arete/dikaiosune) one activity bearing two descriptions.

Cluster 7 (PDF 27-30, book 237-240): Evidence that phantasia accompanies thinking. DA I.1 403a3-10: thinking is bodily-correlated only if it is or involves phantasia. MA 701a5-7, 701a34-36, 701b17-21, 703b18 — the noesis that moves the limbs requires a phantasia-realization. DA III.7 431a14-17: 'to the thinking soul phantasmata serve as aisthemata; the soul never thinks without a phantasma.' DA III.8 432a3-10: 'phantasmata are like aisthemata, only without matter' — the canonical lemma. Animals capable of perceiving are capable of phantasia; many activities of the aisthetikon are also activities of the phantastikon.

Cluster 8 (PDF 31-35, book 241-245): Lexical-historical survey. In Plato (Theaetetus 152b-c, Sophist 235d-236b, Republic 596e-599a, Parmenides 166a, Symposium 211a, Philebus 38c) phantasma is the verbal noun of phainetai meaning 'what appears,' not 'mental image.' Pre-Aristotelian apparition/dream uses (Aeschylus, Euripides, Herodotus) do not lexicalize phantasma = image. Aristotle uses phantasia broadly: EN 1114a32 (phainomenon agathon depends on character); EE 1235b25-29 (phantasia distinct from doxa); Insomn. 460b19 (sun-a-foot-wide); DA 402b22-24 (incidental attributes 'as they appear'). Nussbaum, citing Owen on phainomena, asserts: 'phantasia for Aristotle seems to be as wide-ranging a notion as the notion of the phainomena.'

Cluster 9 (PDF 37-40, book 246-249): Aristotle's apparent commitment to images in the Parva Naturalia (Mem. 450a25-30 zographema, 451a15 phantasma as memory-likeness; Insomn. 461b29 ff. dream as cloud-form residue) is real but limited. (a) The memory passages metaphorize the assimilation to picture-seeing; (b) no informational density is implied; (c) MA 702a5 already shifts to eidola-as-shadows, an awareness of pleasant/painful things 'as no longer extant' that bypasses imaging entirely. The PN theory is theoretically isolable from the action-explanation theory.

Cluster 10 (PDF 41-44, book 250-253): The crux interpretum DA 428a1-4 (the 'kata metaphoran' clause) is reread. Standard reading takes Aristotle to be bracketing the broad phainetai-uses and limiting phantasia to image-cases. Nussbaum objects on three grounds: (1) phantasma need not mean pictorial image; (2) Aristotle continues to use the supposedly excluded broad sense in 428a7, 428a14, 428b2-3, Insomn.; (3) 'kata metaphoran' is Aristotle's standard expression for an extended/transferred sense (oxu of pitch, dunamis in mathematics, andreios used loosely, HA 500a3 + PA 662b25 on horns) — never used to mark off ordinary usage as transferred. Constructive alternative: the 'transferred sense' he is ruling out is the post-Herodotean phantasia = 'mere show, ostentatiousness' (Hdt. VII.10.5, Polybius, Rhet. 1404a11).

Cluster 11 (PDF 45-47, book 254-256): Section III begins. The phantasia/aisthesis identity must be glossed through DA II.12 424a18 ff., where aisthesis 'receives perceptible forms without the matter' as wax receives a signet-ring. Aisthesis is passive impress; what is received are sensible qualities (color, taste, sound) not substances (the rose qua white, not qua rose). But to be moved to action the animal must perceive the substance under a sortal description (cf. Categories 5, Strawson, Wiggins). The 'forms of the pleasant/painful' that phantasia presents (MA 701b21, 703b19-20) are exactly such object-as-F formal contents.

Cluster 12 (PDF 47-50, book 257-260): The voice-passage DA II.8 420b31 ff. is the key piece of evidence: 'that which strikes must be a living creature with some phantasia, for voice is a noise that is semantikos of something.' Voice is meaning-bearing only when the utterer's awareness is directed at an object qua F. Hicks's image-reading is rejected as bizarre — voice would then be semantikos not of the world but of the mental picture. Nussbaum proposes: phantasia is the faculty of object-directed semantic awareness; the De Interpretatione I claim that vocal sounds are sumbola of pathemata is glossed in light of this. Closing formula of Section III: 'There is no receptive innocent eye in perception.'

Cluster 13 (PDF 51-54, book 261-264): Section IV — phantasia/orexis. Examples: thirsty subject sees water-fountain qua drink; the deluded dog sees ammonia qua drink; non-linguistic creatures' phantasia is inferred from behavior + plausible desires. But phantasia is not a behavioral disposition — token-physical descriptions are theoretically available. The two species reappear: perceptual phantasia (shared with animals) vs. deliberative phantasia (bouleutike, 433b28). The crux 434a7-10 ('he is able to make one phantasma out of many') is read against Ross's collage-of-pictures interpretation: deliberative phantasia (1) joins act + consequence into a unified appearing, (2) measures consequence-sets against a single criterion. Phantasia ek syllogismou (434a11) names this rational capacity.

Cluster 14 (PDF 55-58, book 265-267): Section V — phantasia/thinking. DA III.8's strong claim that no thinking is without phantasma is glossed as the empirical thesis that every thought has a concrete symbolic vehicle (image, formalization, words). The Mem. 449b31 triangle example shows the vehicle typically conveys excess detail (a triangle of definite size). 'God would not require phantasia.' Worry: if my judgment that the sun is large must itself be accompanied by some phantasia (the messy overcomplexity worry), then we are forced to insert two phantasiai per judgment — but Aristotle's refusal to physicalize thinking (DA III.5) blocks the simpler solution.

Cluster 15 (PDF 58-59, book 268-269): Closing synthesis. The basic insight underlying Aristotle's theory is that 'perceptual reception is inseparable from interpretation.' Mistaken cordoning of epistemology from action-theory explains the one-sided readings. To move a creature to action an object must appear to him: he must select, mark off, organize, interpret. 'But this is, desire aside, what it is to see it.' The closing aphorism: 'Learning to perceive, as Aristotle tells us, is learning to make distinctions' (citing Metaph. I.1 980b26-27 + Phys. 184a24). Footnote 71: parallel development with Schofield.

concepts.name: Phantasia (Nussbaum's reading)
concepts.definition: The interpretive aspect of perception in virtue of which an animal sees an object as an object of a certain sort — a thing under a formal description that can become an object of pursuit or avoidance. NOT (primarily) the faculty of internal image-having.

concepts.name: Phantasia as 'seeing-as'
concepts.definition: By analogy with Wittgenstein's and Ishiguro's 'seeing-as' / 'seeing an aspect': what phainetai F to someone is what is seen by him as F. Phantasia is the broader Aristotelian counterpart.

concepts.name: Image-view of phantasia (target of critique)
concepts.definition: The interpretation (Ross, Hicks, Hamlyn, Rees, Freudenthal, Sorabji) that phantasia always involves internal images representing by similarity and inspected by the agent.

concepts.name: Phantasma
concepts.definition: Verbal noun of phainesthai. In ordinary Greek = 'what appears'; in restricted Aristotelian usage occasionally = mental likeness/trace (PN), but not by lexical necessity.

concepts.name: Phainesthai / phainetai
concepts.definition: The verb 'to appear / to seem.' Anchors the entire phantasia-family. To say something phainetai F to X is to say X sees it as F.

concepts.name: Phainomena
concepts.definition: Things in the world as seen and reported by sentient observers; in Aristotelian methodology (citing Owen, 'Tithenai ta phainomena'), the explanatory starting-point both in scientific inquiry and in action-theory.

concepts.name: Kritika
concepts.definition: The distinction-making / sorting cognitive faculties (phantasia, aisthesis, nous/dianoia) per MA 6. Their job is to discriminate and present objects under descriptions for the desiring faculty.

concepts.name: Aisthesis (passive impress)
concepts.definition: Reception of sensible form without matter (DA II.12 424a18-19). For Nussbaum, the strictly receptive component of object-awareness — the rose qua white, not qua rose.

concepts.name: Aisthema
concepts.definition: What is received in perception — the form-without-matter impress on the percipient's wax-like sense organ. To be distinguished from phantasma in many uses (e.g., DA 431a14-17: phantasmata serve as aisthemata to the thinking soul).

concepts.name: Orexis
concepts.definition: Desire. Jointly necessary with phantasia for animal motion (DA 432b15). Phantasia prepares desire, which prepares the affections, which prepare the organic parts (MA 702a18 ff.).

concepts.name: Object-as-F (formal content)
concepts.definition: What phantasia adds over aisthesis: the perception of the object under a unitary sortal description ('the man qua man,' 'this qua drink'). The content that can be motivating.

concepts.name: Deliberative phantasia (bouleutike)
concepts.definition: The species of phantasia peculiar to rational creatures (DA III.11 433b28). Capacity to (1) link act + consequence into unified appearing, (2) compare consequence-sets against a single criterion. The substrate of phantasia ek syllogismou.

concepts.name: Perceptual phantasia
concepts.definition: The species of phantasia shared with non-rational animals (DA 433b29-30, 434a6). Single momentary appearings without overall plan; explains incomplete creatures' motion (DA III.11).

concepts.name: Phantasia ek syllogismou
concepts.definition: Phantasia 'from inference' (DA 434a11). The capacity for chained inferential reasoning that distinguishes human deliberation from animal sequential responsiveness.

concepts.name: Same in capacity / different in einai
concepts.definition: Aristotle's formula at DA 433a31 + De Insomn. 459a15: phantasia and aisthesis are the same dunamis under different descriptions. Nussbaum reads this on the arete/dikaiosune model: one capacity, two aspects.

concepts.name: Form without matter (DA 432a9-10)
concepts.definition: The Aristotelian gloss on phantasma: 'phantasmata are like aisthemata, only without matter.' Nussbaum: phantasia involves seeing the object's form (it qua F) where aisthesis would absorb the matter-impress.

concepts.name: Decaying-sense theory
concepts.definition: The minority Aristotelian thesis (DA III.3 closing paragraph; Insomn. 461b29 ff.; Mem. 450a25 ff.) that phantasia consists in residual kineseis set up by past aisthesis, persisting in the object's absence. Nussbaum localizes this to physiological hypothesis, denies its theoretical priority.

concepts.name: Kata metaphoran clause (DA 428a1-4)
concepts.definition: Aristotle's restriction of phantasia at the opening of DA III.3. Standardly read as bracketing the broad phainetai-uses. Nussbaum proposes: bracketing instead the 'mere show / ostentatiousness' sense (Rhet. 1404a11, Hdt. VII.10.5).

concepts.name: Phantasia in our power
concepts.definition: DA 427b17 ff. — phantasia, unlike doxa, is voluntary. Nussbaum reads narrowly (active envisaging) but notes Wittgensteinian parallel: 'seeing an aspect and imagining are subject to the will.'

concepts.name: Phantasia accuracy / falsity
concepts.definition: DA 428a11-12: aisthesis is always (incidentally) accurate, but phantasia can be false. Marks phantasia as interpretive rather than reproductive.

concepts.name: Pistis (distinguishing doxa from phantasia)
concepts.definition: Conviction grounded in experience and logos. DA 428a21-23: doxa requires pistis, which animals lack — hence animals have phantasia but not doxa.

concepts.name: Voice (phone) as semantikos
concepts.definition: DA II.8 420b31 ff. Voice is meaningful noise produced by a living creature 'with phantasia.' Nussbaum's pivotal text: voice is semantikos of an object only because the utterer's awareness is object-directed.

concepts.name: Representation as interpretation
concepts.definition: Anti-similarity thesis (drawing on Goodman's Languages of Art): pictures represent by reference/convention, not by intrinsic resemblance. Picasso-Stein anecdote: representation is interpretation.

concepts.name: Innocent-eye myth
concepts.definition: The myth that there is one 'pure' way of seeing the object, against which all interpretive copies are measured. Nussbaum (citing Goodman): 'representing has always been more a matter of interpreting than of reproducing.'

concepts.name: Token-physicalism of phantasia
concepts.definition: Nussbaum's gloss (S4): phantasia is a psychological process for which a physiological description is theoretically available (token-identical, not type-identical, with bodily change), hence usable in causal explanation.

concepts.name: Phantasia as 'umbrella' faculty
concepts.definition: Aristotle's tendency in action contexts (MA, DA III.9-11) to give phantasia an umbrella role: it functions even when actual aisthesis and noesis are going on.

concepts.name: Symbolic vehicle of thought
concepts.definition: Per DA III.8 432a3-10: every thought has a concrete symbolic accompaniment (image, formalization, words) that supplies a vehicle. 'God would not require phantasia.'

concepts.name: Phantasia and physiology
concepts.definition: Phantasia, like aisthesis, has bodily realization (MA 701b17-21). This is why a non-perceptual thought can move the body: phantasia couples noesis to the somatic motion-apparatus.

concepts.name: Two species of phantasia (DA III.11)
concepts.definition: Aristotle's late distinction (433b28-29) between deliberative/calculative and perceptual phantasia. Nussbaum: not two faculties but two operational ranges of the one phantastikon.

concepts.name: Phainomenon agathon
concepts.definition: The apparent good (EN III.4-5, 1114a32). What appears good to a person depends on what sort of person he is — phantasia is character-relative.

concepts.name: Phantasia vs. doxa
concepts.definition: EE 1235b25-29: pleasure appears good even to those who do not believe it good. Phantasia and doxa are 'not in the same part of the soul' — phantasia is pre-doxastic appearing.

readings.statement: Phantasia is not (primarily) the faculty of having internal pictures; it is the interpretive aspect of perception — the faculty in virtue of which an animal sees an object as an object of a certain sort, where this object-as-F awareness has potentially motivating content. Reception and interpretation are inseparable: there is no 'innocent eye' in Aristotelian aisthesis. Phantasia is roughly Wittgensteinian 'seeing-as,' with scope as wide as that of phainomena.
readings.support_evidence: Lexical kinship phantasia/phainesthai (12-13, 31-36); MA 702a18 ff. phantasia prepares desire (23); DA 433b26-30 no desire without phantasia (23); DA II.12 424a18-19 aisthesis is passive impress, hence cannot supply object-as-F (47-48); 'forms of the pleasant/painful' MA 701b21, 703b19-20 (47); DA II.8 420b31 ff. voice is semantikos only because phantasia is operative (49-50); DA 432a9-10 phantasmata 'without matter' (47 n.52); closing synthesis pp.267-269 (58-59).
readings.contested_by_anticipated: Caston (1996, 1998) will partially extend by stressing intentional content; Schofield (1978/1985) the parallel paper develops a more imagistic and presentational reading; Frede (1992) qualifies by stressing the phantasma side; Wedin (1988) Mind and Imagination in Aristotle resists assimilation to seeing-as. White (1985) is contemporaneous and tends to emphasize the imagistic theory more than Nussbaum allows. O'Gorman, Hawhee, and the rhetorical-studies appropriations after 2000 build on Nussbaum's interpretivism.

readings.statement: The 'decaying-sense' material in DA III.3's closing paragraph and in the Parva Naturalia (Mem. 450a25 ff., Insomn. 461b29 ff.) describes a physiological hypothesis about specific phenomena (memory, dreaming) and cannot be made governing for phantasia generally. DA III.3 itself is internally inconsistent and cannot be the canonical statement of phantasia-theory.
readings.support_evidence: DA III.3's broader uses (428a14, b2-4) presuppose the non-residual interpretive sense (41-42); Mem. 450a25-30 and 451a1 distinguish theorema from phantasma (40); MA 702a5 revises Mem. by treating memory as awareness of pleasant/painful things as eidola/shadows, not as image-having (41); throughout DA III the 'image' is not the operative explanans for phantasia's role in action.
readings.contested_by_anticipated: Sorabji's Aristotle on Memory (1972/2004) — explicitly named at p.12 n.2 — defends the image-theory as canonical. White (1985) and many Anglophone commentators (Wedin) preserve more theoretical weight for the decaying-sense passages.

readings.statement: Aristotle's restriction 'if phantasia is that in virtue of which some phantasma comes-to-be for us, and not what we call phantasia using a transferred sense' should be read as bracketing the post-Herodotean 'mere show / ostentatiousness' sense of phantasia (Rhet. 1404a11), NOT as bracketing the broad phainetai-connected uses. Aristotle's standard use of 'kata metaphoran' marks shifts away from ordinary literal usage; the broad phainetai-sense is the ordinary usage.
readings.support_evidence: Aristotle's consistent use of kata metaphoran elsewhere: musical oxu/baru (DA 420a29), mathematical dunamis (Metaph. 1019b33), loose andreios (EN 1115a15), horns kata metaphoran (HA 500a3, PA 662b25) (43); Rhet. 1404a11 attests phantasia = 'mere show, aimed at the audience'; Aristotle continues to use the broad sense in DA 428a7, a14, b2-3 immediately after (42).
readings.contested_by_anticipated: Most prior commentators (Freudenthal, Hicks, Ross, Hamlyn, Rees) read 428a1-4 as Aristotle's official restriction to the image-cases. Caston, Frede, Wedin all engage this passage and will offer various intermediate readings.

readings.thesis_name: Phantasia/aisthesis identity on the arete/dikaiosune model
readings.statement: Aristotle's claim (DA 433a31, De Insomn. 459a15) that phantasia and aisthesis are 'the same in capacity but different in einai' is best read on the model of arete/dikaiosune (EN V 1130a12) or phronesis/politike (EN VI 1143b23) — one disposition under two descriptions — rather than on the model of road-up/road-down (Metaph. XI.10 1066a33). On this reading, many activities of the aisthetikon are also, under another description, activities of the phantastikon.
readings.support_evidence: Aristotle's terminology phantastikon and aisthetikon (capacity-names, not activity-names) supports the two-description reading (25); the various einai-passages aggregated at pp.25-26; the DA II.12 sortal-vs-quality distinction implies that the same act of perceiving an X-as-F can be redescribed as an act of phantasia.
readings.contested_by_anticipated: Schofield's parallel paper holds a more presentational/imagistic distinction; Wedin (Mind and Imagination 1988) resists full identity. The contemporary debate (Caston, Frede, Lorenz) continues to argue over whether phantasia is a sub-capacity of aisthesis or a logically distinct faculty co-housed with it.

readings.statement: Aristotle's claim that the rational deliberator 'makes one phantasma out of many' (434a7-10) does NOT mean Ross's collage-of-pictures (an internal montage assembled from sub-images). It means: the rational creature can (1) see an action's consequences as following from it — joining two appearings as a unity — and (2) measure consequence-sets against a single criterion of goodness/desirability. The 'phantasia ek syllogismou' (434a11) is inferential, not pictorial.
readings.support_evidence: 434a7-10 in context (53-54); the cloak example from MA 7 (54); the fact that goodness, the criterion measured against, is not pictorially representable (53); DA III.7 431b6-8 ('when one calculates, using the phantasmata or noemata in the soul, as if one saw the things') admits picturing but is non-committal as to whether all deliberation is pictorial.
readings.contested_by_anticipated: Ross (commentary on DA), Hicks, Hamlyn. Modern philosophy-of-action readings (Cooper, Charles, Broadie) will engage this passage extensively.

readings.thesis_name: All thought requires phantasma as concrete symbolic vehicle
readings.statement: DA III.8 432a3-10's claim that 'the soul never thinks without a phantasma' should be read as the empirical thesis that every act of thinking is accompanied by some concrete vehicle of symbolizing or envisaging (an image, a formalization, words) — not as the metaphysical claim that thought IS imaging. 'God would not require phantasia.' The Mem. 449b31 ff. triangle example illustrates: the symbolizing typically conveys excess information (a triangle of definite size).
readings.contested_by_anticipated: This is one of the most contested doctrines. Caston, Wedin, Frede, Modrak, Lorenz all engage. Burnyeat's 'Is an Aristotelian Philosophy of Mind Still Credible?' (1992) takes a strong line that conflicts at certain points.

tensions.name: DA III.3 internally inconsistent
tensions.description: DA III.3 mixes a broad, phainetai-connected, error-explaining account of phantasia (427b17 ff., 428a14 ff., the sun-example) with a closing decaying-sense paragraph (429a1 ff.) on residual kineseis. Nussbaum insists these cannot both be the chapter's official theory; the broad scope must be preserved over the narrow technical close.

tensions.name: Two-aspect vs. two-activity reading of phantasia/aisthesis identity
tensions.description: Whether DA 433a31's claim that phantasia and aisthesis are 'one but different in einai' is to be read on the road-up/road-down model (two distinct activities of one power) or the arete/dikaiosune model (one activity, two descriptions). Nussbaum prefers the latter but admits Aristotle's evidence is mixed.

tensions.name: Active phantasia vs. passive aisthesis sometimes blurred
tensions.description: Although DA II.12 makes aisthesis fully passive, DA II.5 and some other passages give aisthesis an active, interpretive role of its own. This complicates Nussbaum's clean division of labor between phantasia (interpretation) and aisthesis (impress).

tensions.name: Image-language in the Mem. triangle case and PN passages
tensions.description: At Mem. 449b31 ff. the triangle envisaging is explicitly pictorial ('places before his eyes'); the PN dream and memory passages do invoke similarity-bearing kineseis. Nussbaum concedes that imaging finds a place within the theory but resists making it theoretically central.

tensions.name: The 'extra phantasia' overcomplexity
tensions.description: If a judgment opposing a sensory phantasia must itself be accompanied by a phantasia (to be physiologically realized), we are committed to multiplying phantasiai per cognitive episode. The simpler functionalist solution is blocked by DA III.5's commitment to nous as separable.

tensions.name: Phantasia ascribed inconsistently to lower animals
tensions.description: DA 425a10 ff. tentatively denies phantasia to the worm; DA III.11 extends it to all self-movers; DA 415a10 ff. allows some phtharta to lack it. Aristotle has no settled position on the scope of phantasia-possession.

tensions.name: DA 428a1-4 kata metaphoran clause is overdetermined
tensions.description: The standard reading takes the bracketed sense to be the broad phainetai-uses; Nussbaum's rereading takes it to be the 'mere show' sense. Both can be defended grammatically; Aristotle's silence on which transferred sense he means leaves the question open.
